name: Collagen filler

lead: Collagen fillers are injected into the skin to smooth lines and add volume. Bovine collagen (Zyderm, Zyplast) was the leading filler in the US for about two decades and was long treated as the gold standard before hyaluronic acid products took over.
The effect is temporary. Forums rarely discuss collagen injections today, and mentions of collagen mostly concern supplements.

paras: The injected collagen physically adds volume under a wrinkle or fold and is gradually absorbed by the body.

Reviews note hypersensitivity reactions with bovine collagen, and the FDA advises allergy screening for fillers containing collagen. As with all fillers, bruising, swelling and lumps can occur; results are temporary.

lead: Collagen fillers are injectable implants made from animal-derived or human bioengineered collagen, used to soften wrinkles and fold lines and to add soft-tissue volume. They are generally regarded as the original modern injectable dermal filler: a 2006 review notes that bovine collagen was the most popular injectable implant in the United States for nearly two decades before human bioengineered collagen products and hyaluronic acid fillers became available [1].

A 2001 review described injectable Zyderm bovine collagen as having come to be regarded as the gold standard against which other fillers were measured [2]. The correction is temporary, and bovine products can cause hypersensitivity reactions, which was the context for a randomised trial comparing hyaluronic acid (Restylane) with bovine collagen (Zyplast) in the nasolabial folds [3].

Collagen fillers have since been largely displaced in many markets by hyaluronic acid, though newer collagen-based and recombinant-collagen products continue to be registered for study [4][5][6]. The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of collagen injections as a filler; forum mentions of collagen concern dietary supplements.

paras: A review of collagen fillers outlines the injectable collagen implants available, including animal- and human-derived types, along with injection techniques, preferred treatment methods and possible adverse reactions [1]. Wikipedia notes that glutaraldehyde crosslinking has been used with collagen-based fillers to improve their integration [7].

Bovine collagen was the dominant injectable for roughly two decades in the US before alternatives appeared, according to a 2006 review [1]. Dermal fillers in general became widely used from the 1980s [7]. Human bioengineered collagen products and hyaluronic acid fillers followed [1].

The cited trial literature describes bovine collagen as giving only temporary correction and as capable of causing hypersensitivity reactions [3]. The FDA's dermal filler guidance notes that some fillers contain collagen or egg-derived products, so people with relevant allergies should be screened. Allergy and adverse-response considerations are a stated topic of reviews of collagen substances [2].

A randomised, double-blind, multicentre comparison of Restylane (non-animal stabilised hyaluronic acid) with Zyplast (bovine collagen) for nasolabial folds was published in 2003 [3]; the figures are not reproduced here.

Registered studies of collagen-containing dermal products include a trial of a collagen dermal filler with lidocaine for nasolabial folds (240 participants), a phase 3 trial of a collagen filler for crow's feet (260 participants, not yet recruiting), and a premarketing trial of a filler combining hyaluronic acid and recombinant collagen [4][5][6]. A phase 3 comparison of TheraFill with Koken on nasolabial folds (73 participants) is also registered [8].
